idea: Comparing fractions means deciding which of two fractions is larger, smaller, or whether they are equal. A fraction tells us how many equal parts we have (the numerator) and how big each part is (the denominator). If the parts are the same size, or the number of parts is the same, the comparison is easy. Otherwise we rewrite the fractions so they can be compared fairly, or we use a benchmark like 1/2.
why: Two amounts can only be compared fairly when they are measured in the same unit. With the same denominator the pieces are the same size, so more pieces means more. With the same numerator we have the same number of pieces, so bigger pieces (a smaller denominator) means more. When both numbers differ, we rewrite each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator. Multiplying top and bottom by the same number does not change the value, because it is multiplying by 1. Now the pieces are the same size and we compare the numerators. A benchmark such as 1/2 is a shortcut: if one fraction is below 1/2 and the other above it, the order is already clear.

theory_example.steps: The denominators 3 and 5 differ, so find a common denominator: 3 x 5 = 15. Rewrite 2/3 = (2x5)/(3x5) = 10/15. Rewrite 3/5 = (3x3)/(5x3) = 9/15. Now both are in fifteenths, so compare numerators: 10 > 9. So 2/3 > 3/5.

lesson_outline.activity: Warm-up: ask 'Would you rather have 1/2 or 1/4 of the same chocolate bar?' Let students explain why. Name the goal: decide which fraction is bigger and give a reason.
Teach 'Same denominator or same numerator'. Draw the bars on the board, work the example, then ask the check question.
Teach 'Common denominator'. Work the example 3/4 vs 5/6 slowly, step by step, then ask the check question. Let students say each step aloud.
Teach 'Benchmarks: compare with 1/2'. Work the example, then ask the check question. Remind students this is a shortcut, not the only method.
Extra examples and questions round: work the 3 extra examples together, letting students choose which method to use and say why. Leave time for their questions.

ways_to_explain.text: Draw two identical bars, each cut into 8 equal parts. Shade 3 parts on one and 5 on the other. The parts are the same size, so the bar with more shaded parts has more: 5/8 > 3/8. Then draw two identical bars, one cut into 4 parts and one into 7, and shade 3 parts of each. The 4-part bar has bigger parts, so 3/4 > 3/7.

Two friends each get slices of identical pizzas cut into 8 slices. One eats 3 slices, the other 5. Who ate more? The one with 5. Now one pizza is cut into 4 slices and another into 7, and each friend eats 3 slices. Cutting into fewer slices makes bigger slices, so 3 slices of the 4-slice pizza is more.

example.steps: Same denominator 8: the pieces are the same size, so compare numerators: 5 > 3, so 5/8 > 3/8. Same numerator 3: we have the same number of pieces, so the bigger pieces win. Fourths are bigger than sevenths, so 3/4 > 3/7.

mistakes.mistake: Students think a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction, e.g. 1/7 > 1/4 because 7 > 4.
mistakes.response: Go back to the pizza: cutting into more slices makes smaller slices. Have them draw 1/4 and 1/7 of the same bar and look.

mistakes.mistake: With the same numerator, students compare the denominators the wrong way round, or say the fractions are equal because the tops match.
mistakes.response: Ask 'same number of pieces, but are the pieces the same size?' Draw it so they see the sizes differ.

student_questions.question: But why is 1/8 smaller than 1/4 when 8 is bigger?
student_questions.answer: The denominator tells how many equal pieces the whole is cut into. More pieces means each piece is smaller, so an eighth is smaller than a fourth.

student_questions.question: Can I just compare the top numbers?
student_questions.answer: Only when the bottom numbers are the same. Then the pieces are the same size, so counting pieces tells you which is more.

student_questions.question: What if the tops and bottoms are both different?
student_questions.answer: Good question, that is the next part. We rewrite them so the bottoms match, or use a benchmark.

check_question.question: Which is larger, 4/9 or 4/5?
check_question.solution: The numerators are the same (4), so compare piece size. Fifths are bigger than ninths, so 4/5 is larger.

ways_to_explain.text: 1) Find a common denominator, a number both denominators divide into (their product always works; the smallest one is tidier). 2) Multiply the top and bottom of each fraction by whatever turns its denominator into that number. 3) Compare the numerators. 4) Give the answer in terms of the original fractions.

Draw two equal bars. Cut one into 4 parts and the other into 6. Then cut both into 12 parts: each fourth becomes 3 twelfths and each sixth becomes 2 twelfths. Now 3/4 shows as 9 twelfths and 5/6 as 10 twelfths, and the pieces are the same size, so you can count them.

example.steps: Denominators 4 and 6 both divide into 12, so use 12. 3/4 = (3x3)/(4x3) = 9/12. 5/6 = (5x2)/(6x2) = 10/12. Compare numerators: 10 > 9, so 5/6 > 3/4. The difference is 1/12.

mistakes.mistake: Students change only the denominator and leave the numerator, e.g. writing 3/4 as 3/12.
mistakes.response: Remind them that what we do to the bottom we must do to the top, because we multiply by 1 (3/3). Use the bar picture to show 3/4 is 9/12.

mistakes.mistake: Students say the answer is the larger numerator, e.g. 'the answer is 10/12', or forget to go back to the original fractions.
mistakes.response: Ask 'Which of the original fractions is this?' The 10/12 is 5/6, so the answer is 5/6. Twelfths were only a helper.

student_questions.question: Why does changing 3/4 to 9/12 not change its value?
student_questions.answer: We multiplied by 3/3, which is 1. The same amount is cut into smaller pieces, and we count three times as many.

student_questions.question: Do I have to use the smallest common denominator?
student_questions.answer: No. Any common denominator works, for example 24 here. The smallest one just keeps the numbers small.

student_questions.question: Is there a faster way?
student_questions.answer: Yes: cross-multiply, 3x6 = 18 and 5x4 = 20. But it is the same idea in disguise, since it compares numerators over the common denominator 24. Understand the common denominator first.

ways_to_explain.text: Ask 'Is this fraction less than, equal to, or more than 1/2?' A fraction is less than 1/2 when double the numerator is less than the denominator, equal when double equals the denominator, and more when double is greater. If the two fractions land on different sides of 1/2, the order is clear.

Imagine a water bottle. 4/9 of a bottle is a little less than half full, and 5/8 is more than half full. You can tell which is fuller without any calculating, just by asking which side of half-full each one is on.

example.steps: Half of 9 is 4.5, and 4 < 4.5, so 4/9 is less than 1/2. Half of 8 is 4, and 5 > 4, so 5/8 is more than 1/2. Since one is below 1/2 and the other above, 5/8 is larger.

mistakes.mistake: Students think any fraction with a small numerator is less than 1/2, e.g. 3/4 or 2/3 can't be bigger than 1/2 because 3 and 2 are small.
mistakes.response: The numerator must be compared with half the denominator. Ask them to double the numerator and compare it with the denominator.

mistakes.mistake: Students use the benchmark when both fractions are on the same side of 1/2 and then guess.
mistakes.response: Tell them the benchmark only decides when the fractions are on different sides. Otherwise switch to a common denominator.

student_questions.question: Why 1/2? Can we use other benchmarks?
student_questions.answer: 1/2 is easy to picture and test. You can also use 0 or 1, for example to see which fraction is closer to a whole.

student_questions.question: What if one is exactly 1/2?
student_questions.answer: Then check the other one. If it is more than 1/2, it wins. If it is also on the same side, use a common denominator.

student_questions.question: What if both are more than 1/2?
student_questions.answer: Then the benchmark does not settle it. Use a common denominator.

check_question.question: Which is larger, 3/8 or 4/7?
check_question.solution: Half of 8 is 4 and 3 < 4, so 3/8 is below 1/2. Half of 7 is 3.5 and 4 > 3.5, so 4/7 is above 1/2. So 4/7 is larger.

extra_examples.solution: Use 20 as a common denominator. 7/10 = 14/20 and 3/4 = 15/20. Since 15 > 14, 3/4 is larger.
The numerators are the same, so compare piece size. Ninths are bigger than twelfths, so 5/9 is larger.

Use 56 as a common denominator. 6/7 = 48/56 and 7/8 = 49/56. Since 49 > 48, 7/8 is larger. (Another way: each is 1 piece short of a whole, and an eighth is smaller than a seventh, so 7/8 is closer to 1.)
